Lesson 01 / 08

Why Is Human Language Difficult for Machines?

In this lesson
  • 1. The five levels of language we'll work with
  • 2. Morphology — Words have internal structure
  • 3. Syntax — The relationship between words
  • 4. Semantics — What does the sentence actually mean?
  • 5. Structural ambiguity — Sometimes even the grammar is uncertain
  • 6. Pragmatics — Meaning depends on the situation
  • 7. Discourse — Language extends beyond one sentence
  • 8. Our first NLP experiment — Why word counts lose meaning
  • 9. Where does our neural-network knowledge fit?
  • 10. A crucial research issue: What counts as the correct interpretation?
  • 11. Check your understanding
  • 12. Final mental model
  • The discovery that leads to Lesson 2

Language structure · Morphology · Syntax · Semantics · Pragmatics · Ambiguity

We've already learned how a Transformer processes tokens:

Token IDs

Embeddings

Transformer

Predictions

But this raises a more fundamental question:

What information must those vectors and transformations represent for the model to do something meaningful with language?

Consider these two sentences:

SENTENCE A

The dog chased the cat.

Dog Cat

SENTENCE B

The cat chased the dog.

Cat Dog

They contain exactly the same words, but describe different events.

A machine that simply counts words would represent them identically. A machine that understands their grammatical roles could distinguish who chased whom.

That's our first discovery:

Human language isn't just a collection of words. Meaning also depends on structure, context and intention.

We'll unpack these dimensions one by one.

1. The five levels of language we'll work with

Linguistics provides useful ways of studying language at different levels.

These aren't five mandatory processing stages. They're five complementary ways to describe the information an NLP system may need.

Some classical NLP pipelines explicitly analyze them. Modern neural models often learn useful aspects of them implicitly from training data.

2. Morphology — Words have internal structure

Let's begin with individual words.

Consider:

Example: "unhelpful"

un

Prefix

help

Root

ful

Suffix

These meaningful parts are called morphemes. This example combines a negative prefix, a root and an adjective-forming suffix.

Two particularly important kinds of morphology are:

Type Example What changes?
Inflection walk → walked Grammatical form, such as tense
Derivation help → helpful Word meaning or grammatical category

Why does this matter for NLP?

Imagine a training corpus containing:

connect, connected, connecting, connection, reconnect

An algorithm treating each spelling as a completely unrelated word may fail to exploit their shared structure.

This motivates several approaches we'll study later:

  • Word normalization and lemmatization.
  • Subword tokenization.
  • Character-based representations.
  • Morphology-aware language modeling.

Connection to neural networks: Whether the model receives whole-word tokens, subword tokens or individual characters changes what information its embedding layer must learn.

We'll return to this in Lesson 2.

3. Syntax — The relationship between words

Now we understand that words have internal structure. But individual words still aren't enough to interpret a sentence.

Return to:

"The cat chased the dog."

A useful grammatical analysis identifies:

  • cat — subject of chased
  • chased — main verb
  • dog — object of chased

One way NLP represents these relationships is through a dependency tree.

Dependency structure

Simplified dependency tree, omitting the determiner words "The" and "the".

In a dependency parse, words are nodes and grammatical relationships are edges.

The labels describe what role each word plays.

If we swap "cat" and "dog", their grammatical roles change even though the set of words stays the same.

Parts of speech (POS)

POS tagging assigns grammatical categories to tokens.

Token POS Interpretation
The DET Determiner
cat NOUN Noun
chased VERB Verb
the DET Determiner
dog NOUN Noun
. PUNCT Punctuation

A POS tagger answers questions like: Is this word functioning as a noun, verb, adjective or determiner in this context?

This is important because the same spelling can have different grammatical roles.

For example:

  • "I book a ticket." — verb
  • "I read a book." — noun

Why syntax matters for our NLP models

Imagine an argument-identification system analyzing:

"The proposal reduces pollution."

versus:

"Pollution reduces the proposal."

The same major content words occur, but the grammatical relationships—and plausibility—differ.

Syntax helps distinguish the roles that entities and actions play.

However, syntax by itself isn't sufficient for understanding meaning. That brings us to our next level.

4. Semantics — What does the sentence actually mean?

Syntax tells us how words are organized.

Semantics concerns what words and their combinations mean.

Consider the word bank.

Interactive: Same word, different meaning

“The bank approved the loan.”

Likely meaning: financial institution. Context clues: approved, loan.

This is lexical ambiguity: one word form has multiple possible interpretations.

The task of choosing an appropriate meaning in context is called Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD).

We can express its goal conceptually as:

m^=arg⁡max⁡mP(m∣w,c)\boxed{\hat m=\arg\max_m P(m\mid w,c)}

Where:

  • ww is the word.
  • cc is its context.
  • mm is a candidate meaning.

This isn't a requirement that all systems explicitly calculate these probabilities. It's a way to formalize the task.

Meaning also depends on how words combine

Consider:

"All students passed."

"Not all students passed."

Only one word changes, but the logical meaning changes substantially.

This is an example of compositional semantics: meaning depends on how the meanings of individual expressions are combined.

A model must often learn how negation, quantifiers, roles and other structures affect interpretation.

This is why simply finding keywords isn't sufficient for many NLP tasks.

5. Structural ambiguity — Sometimes even the grammar is uncertain

Consider this sentence:

"I saw her duck."

There are at least two interpretations.

Interpretation 1

I saw the duck belonging to her.

"duck" functions as a noun.

Interpretation 2

I saw her lower her head.

"duck" functions as a verb.

This is more than a single word having two meanings.

The sentence can also be analyzed with different grammatical structures.

In interpretation 1, "her duck" is a noun phrase. In interpretation 2, "her" is the person observed performing the action "duck."

Important insight: Syntax and semantics influence one another. We often need both to determine which interpretation is intended.

Some ambiguous sentences remain unresolved even with substantial context. NLP systems shouldn't always pretend there is one certain interpretation.

6. Pragmatics — Meaning depends on the situation

Now we've reached something more subtle.

Consider:

"Could you open the window?"

Its literal grammatical form is a question about someone's ability.

But in ordinary conversation, its intended function is usually a request.

Literal sentence meaning

Is the listener capable of opening the window?

Likely communicative intention

Please open the window.

Pragmatics examines how language is used in context, including speaker intentions, conversational expectations and implied meaning.

Another example:

"It's getting cold in here."

Depending on the situation, that might be:

  • An observation.
  • An indirect request to close a window.
  • A complaint about the heating.

The words alone don't fully determine the intended action.

Why does this matter for NLP?

Imagine a chatbot designed to classify customer requests.

If someone says:

"I wonder whether you could refund this order."

A purely surface-level classifier might treat it as an expression of curiosity.

A pragmatic interpretation identifies a likely refund request.

That distinction matters when NLP systems interact with people rather than simply categorize isolated sentences.

7. Discourse — Language extends beyond one sentence

Most real documents contain connected sentences, not isolated examples.

Consider:

"Sara called Maya. She was upset."

Who was upset?

Possibly Sara. Possibly Maya.

The pronoun "she" requires interpretation in relation to the preceding sentence, and the information provided doesn't settle the question.

This illustrates coreference resolution: identifying expressions that refer to the same entity.

Two possible referents. The ambiguity may require additional discourse context to resolve.

Discourse analysis also studies how sentences relate logically or rhetorically.

For example:

"The train was delayed. Therefore, we missed the meeting."

The second sentence expresses a consequence of the first.

And:

"Public transport reduces congestion. Therefore, cities should invest in it."

Here we have evidence followed by a recommendation, which connects to argument structure.

These relationships may extend over multiple paragraphs.

The bigger picture: Five sources of information

What an NLP model may need to infer

Discourse relationships

How do entities, events and arguments connect across sentences?

These dimensions overlap and interact. A useful NLP system may represent them explicitly, implicitly, or through some combination of both.

8. Our first NLP experiment — Why word counts lose meaning

Let's write a tiny piece of Python.

We'll represent two sentences by the frequencies of their words.

Python
import re
from collections import Counter

sentence_a = "The dog chased the cat."
sentence_b = "The cat chased the dog."

def tokenize(text):
    return re.findall(r"[a-z]+", text.lower())

tokens_a = tokenize(sentence_a)
tokens_b = tokenize(sentence_b)

bow_a = Counter(tokens_a)
bow_b = Counter(tokens_b)

print("Sentence A:", tokens_a)
print("Sentence B:", tokens_b)

print("Same Bag-of-Words?", bow_a == bow_b)
# True

print("Bag-of-Words:", bow_a)
# Counter({'the': 2, 'dog': 1, 'chased': 1, 'cat': 1})

We've discovered a problem.

Our simple Bag-of-Words representation cannot distinguish the sentences because the two word-frequency vectors are identical.

Yet the meaning differs.

This isn't a bug in Python. It's information loss caused by the representation.

The representation keeps which words occur and how often, but discards their order and grammatical relationships.

A second experiment: A basic rule for "bank"

Python
def guess_bank_meaning(sentence):
    words = set(tokenize(sentence))

    if {"loan", "approved"} & words:
        return "financial institution"

    if {"river", "fisherman"} & words:
        return "river bank"

    return "unknown"

examples = [
    "The bank approved the loan.",
    "The fisherman rested on the river bank.",
    "The bank opened early."
]

for sentence in examples:
    print(sentence)
    print("Predicted:", guess_bank_meaning(sentence))

Our hand-written rules work on some examples.

But what about:

"The bank opened early."

The sentence probably refers to a financial institution in many contexts, but our rule returns unknown.

And the phrase "river bank loan" could confuse our rules in other settings.

We could continue adding rules, but real language contains too many contexts, exceptions and ambiguities for a small keyword system to handle reliably.

That's a major motivation for statistical and machine-learning approaches.

Instead of explicitly writing every rule, we try to learn useful patterns and representations from data.

9. Where does our neural-network knowledge fit?

We now have two complementary views.

Classical NLP approach (illustrative)

Raw text

Tokenization + engineered linguistic features

Statistical classifier or other model

Modern contextual neural approach

Raw text

Tokenization → Token IDs → Embeddings

Transformer produces contextual representations

Prediction head / generation

Classical NLP methods can incorporate learned features too, and modern models can also use explicit linguistic information. The two aren't mutually exclusive.

The key distinction is that contemporary contextual language models can learn representations in which the same token has different contextualized vectors depending on its surrounding text.

For example, the token "bank" can begin from the same token embedding but acquire different contextual representations through attention when surrounded by "loan" versus "river."

So we don't always need a separate word-sense disambiguation rule. The model can potentially learn to use context.

Of course, that doesn't mean it always interprets language correctly.

10. A crucial research issue: What counts as the correct interpretation?

Remember our sentence:

"I saw her duck."

Without additional context, there are multiple legitimate interpretations.

If a dataset assigns only one label, the model may be penalized for another plausible interpretation.

This leads to a broader NLP lesson:

A dataset label isn't always a context-free linguistic truth.

It may reflect:

  • A particular annotation guideline.
  • The context supplied to annotators.
  • A task-specific definition.
  • A simplification of a genuinely ambiguous phenomenon.

For example, whether a sentence counts as an argument can depend on how the task defines claims, evidence, premises and argumentative context.

This is why we'll eventually study annotation guidelines, inter-annotator agreement, dataset shift and evaluation. These are not merely administrative details—they affect what the model is learning.

11. Check your understanding

Consider these two sentences:

"The teacher praised the student."

"The student praised the teacher."

Why can't a simple Bag-of-Words representation distinguish their meanings?

Answer and explanation

B. Bag-of-Words discards order and grammatical roles. Both sentences have the same word counts, even though the teacher and student exchange roles.

12. Final mental model

1. Morphology — What's inside a word?

Prefixes, roots, suffixes and grammatical forms.

2. Syntax — How do words relate?

Word order, grammatical categories and dependency structures.

3. Semantics — What does the expression mean?

Word senses, compositional meaning, negation and interpretation.

4. Pragmatics — What does the speaker intend?

Requests, implications and context-dependent communication.

5. Discourse — How does language connect across sentences?

Reference, coherence, relations and argument structure.

The discovery that leads to Lesson 2

We've established that an NLP system may need to recognize words, grammatical relationships, meanings and context.

But our neural networks can't directly calculate weighted sums over letters and words as abstract symbols.

They operate on numbers.

So before we can train an NLP model, we need to decide:

What is the fundamental unit of text that we represent numerically?

A character? A word? A meaningful word part? Something else?

For example, should we represent:

unbelievable

as:

Word

unbelievable

Subwords

Characters

The subword segmentation is illustrative; actual tokenizer output depends on its vocabulary and algorithm.

Each choice changes the vocabulary, sequence length, representation and learning problem.

That brings us naturally to Lesson 2 — Text Processing, Tokenization and Vocabulary Construction, where we'll build our first real NLP preprocessing pipeline and discover why modern language models rely so heavily on subword tokenization.

From raw language to numerical representations · Word, character and subword tokenization · BPE · WordPiece · Unigram

In Lesson 1, we discovered that language has several layers of structure:

  • Morphology: Words contain meaningful parts.

  • Syntax: Word order and grammatical relationships matter.

  • Semantics: Meaning depends on context.

  • Pragmatics and discourse: Interpretation can depend on intention and surrounding sentences.

We ended with an important question:

If neural networks only perform mathematical operations on numbers, how do we convert human language into something they can process?

That's our problem today.

We'll follow one sentence through a complete NLP input pipeline, then build several tokenizers ourselves and examine the trade-offs.

1. From a sentence to a Transformer

Take our familiar example:

The bank approved the loan.

Our neural network cannot directly multiply the word "bank" by a weight matrix.

First, we need to choose the units of text, assign them numerical identifiers and convert those identifiers into vectors.

Raw text

"The bank approved the loan."

Text processing

Unicode handling, optional normalization, segmentation

Tokenization

The

bank

approved

the

loan

.

Vocabulary lookup → Token IDs

[4, 5, 6, 4, 7, 8]

Illustrative vocabulary with lowercasing

Embedding lookup

Each ID → a learned vector of D numbers

Neural network / Transformer

Contextual representations → Task predictions

Notice that tokenization and embedding are different operations.

Tokenization decides where to divide the text and assigns token IDs. Embedding maps those IDs into numerical vectors.

Let's understand each step.

2. Text preprocessing — Should we modify the original text?

Before tokenizing, we often need to make decisions about how to handle the raw text.

For example:

Original

Possible normalization

HELLO

hello

Hello!!!

hello

Multiple spacesSingle spaces
Different Unicode representationsConsistent Unicode form

You might think: Why not always lowercase everything, remove punctuation and clean away the unnecessary details?

Because sometimes those details carry meaning.

Consider:

"I like this."

"I LIKE THIS!!!"

The words are nearly identical, but capitalization and punctuation may convey additional emphasis.

Or:

"This is good."

"This is not good."

Removing a common word such as "not" could reverse the meaning.

Preprocessing decisions depend on the task

Operation

Potential benefit

Potential problem

Lowercasing

Smaller vocabulary

Loses capitalization distinctions

Removing punctuation

Simpler features

Loses sentence boundaries and signals

Removing stopwords

Smaller sparse representations

May remove negation or useful syntax

Stemming

Groups related word forms

Can produce unnatural fragments

Lemmatization

Maps inflections to dictionary forms

Requires linguistic analysis; may lose grammatical information

Unicode normalization

Consistent representation

Some normalization forms change distinctions

For classical Bag-of-Words systems, stronger normalization may sometimes be useful.

For modern pretrained Transformers, we normally use the preprocessing expected by that model's tokenizer, rather than arbitrarily applying additional transformations.

Here's a minimal example:

Python
import unicodedata

text = "The BANK approved the loan!!!"

# Standardize Unicode composition
normalized = unicodedata.normalize("NFC", text)

# Optional lowercasing for our toy experiment
lowercased = normalized.lower()

print(normalized)
print(lowercased)

One subtle issue: Unicode text can contain visually identical sequences represented by different underlying code points.

Unicode normalization helps make those representations consistent.

For our course, we'll initially use simple, clean English examples, but later we'll discuss why multilingual text, emojis, code and irregular spelling complicate tokenization.

3. Word tokenization — Our first approach

The simplest idea is:

Split a sentence into words.

Suppose we have:

The bank approved the loan.

A basic word tokenizer might produce:

["The", "bank", "approved", "the", "loan", "."]

Notice that the period can be treated as a separate token.

A simple Python tokenizer

Python
import re

def word_tokenize(text):
    return re.findall(
        r"\w+|[^\w\s]",
        text.lower()
    )

sentence = "The bank approved the loan."

tokens = word_tokenize(sentence)

print(tokens)
# ['the', 'bank', 'approved', 'the', 'loan', '.']

This is a useful starting point, not a complete linguistic tokenizer. For example, contractions such as "don't" require more careful handling, and many languages do not mark word boundaries with spaces.

What is a token?

A token is a unit defined by a tokenizer.

It may be:

  • A word.

  • A punctuation mark.

  • A subword fragment.

  • A character.

  • A byte or byte sequence represented through the tokenizer's vocabulary.

A token is not necessarily a whole word or meaningful morpheme.

This distinction becomes crucial when we study modern language models.

4. Vocabulary construction — Turning tokens into integers

We now have tokens, but our neural network still needs numbers.

Let's create a vocabulary.

A vocabulary is a mapping between tokens and unique integer IDs.

For example:

Token

ID

<PAD>

0

<UNK>

1

<BOS>

2

<EOS>

3

the

4

bank

5

approved

6

loan

7

.

8

The tokenized sentence becomes:

[4,5,6,4,7,8][4,5,6,4,7,8]

If we include sequence boundary tokens:

[2,4,5,6,4,7,8,3]\boxed{[2,4,5,6,4,7,8,3]}

What are the special tokens?

  • <PAD>: Fills unused positions when batching sequences of different lengths.

  • <UNK>: Represents a token not present in the vocabulary.

  • <BOS>: Marks the beginning of a sequence.

  • <EOS>: Marks the end of a sequence.

Other systems may have mask tokens, separator tokens, role markers or other special tokens. Not every model uses the same set.

Build our vocabulary in Python

We'll use a small corpus that connects to our first lecture.

Python
corpus = [
    "The bank approved the loan.",
    "The river bank was muddy.",
    "The dog chased the cat.",
    "The cat chased the dog.",
    "The worker was unhappy.",
    "The workers were helpful."
]

special_tokens = [
    "<PAD>", "<UNK>", "<BOS>", "<EOS>"
]

# Create vocabulary from observed training text
all_tokens = sorted({
    token
    for sentence in corpus
    for token in word_tokenize(sentence)
})

vocab = special_tokens + all_tokens

stoi = {token: i for i, token in enumerate(vocab)}
itos = {i: token for token, i in stoi.items()}

def encode_words(text):
    tokens = word_tokenize(text)

    return (
        [stoi["<BOS>"]]
        + [stoi.get(t, stoi["<UNK>"]) for t in tokens]
        + [stoi["<EOS>"]]
    )

sentence = "The bank approved the loan."

ids = encode_words(sentence)

print("Vocabulary size:", len(vocab))
print("Token IDs:", ids)
print("Decoded tokens:", [itos[i] for i in ids])

We've now built our first actual text-to-integer pipeline.

A crucial distinction

Token IDs are labels, not numerical measurements.

If bank has ID 5 and loan has ID 7, that does not mean loan is numerically larger or semantically closer to token 8.

These integer IDs are used to select rows from an embedding matrix.

For example, with vocabulary size VV and embedding dimension DD:

E∈RV×DE\in\mathbb R^{V\times D}

And:

Embedding⁡(5)=E[5]\boxed{\operatorname{Embedding}(5)=E[5]}

The embedding matrix contains learnable numbers.

That's the direct connection to the neural-network architectures from Deep Learning Architectures.

5. Our first problem: What happens to unseen words?

Our vocabulary only contains words observed in the training corpus.

Now imagine the model receives:

"The workers were unhelpful."

The word unhelpful doesn't appear in our original corpus.

Our word-level tokenizer can identify it as a word, but the vocabulary lookup returns:

<UNK>

This is called the out-of-vocabulary (OOV) problem.

Let's think about why that's wasteful.

We've already encountered words such as:

  • help

  • helpful

  • unhappy

  • unhelpful

  • unhelpfulness

These share meaningful pieces, yet a whole-word vocabulary may treat each as a separate entry.

One solution is to make our tokens smaller.

Three possible representations

Interactive tokenizer comparison

Resulting tokens · 4

unhelpfulness
WordSubwordCharacter
1413

These subword segmentations are illustrative and morphology-inspired. A real BPE, WordPiece or Unigram tokenizer may produce different pieces.

Each approach offers a different trade-off.

Approach

Advantage

Limitation

Words

Short sequences, familiar units

Large vocabulary, OOV problem

Characters

Can represent words built from known characters

Much longer sequences

Subwords

Reuse common fragments, balance vocabulary and length

Segmentation may not match linguistic word parts

Character tokenizers are only guaranteed to represent characters within their supported character set. A byte-based tokenizer can go further by representing arbitrary encoded text using a fixed byte alphabet.

Why does sequence length matter?

Remember our Transformer lesson: standard self-attention creates a T×TT\times T attention-score matrix.

If one representation requires 5 tokens and another requires 20, the latter involves many more token-pair attention scores.

On the other hand, an enormous vocabulary requires a large embedding table and potentially a large output projection.

So tokenizer design involves balancing vocabulary size, sequence length, coverage and computational cost.

6. Subword tokenization — How can a tokenizer learn useful pieces?

Instead of manually choosing prefixes and suffixes, we can learn a subword vocabulary from a corpus.

A particularly important algorithm is Byte Pair Encoding (BPE).

The original idea is simple:

Start with small symbols and repeatedly merge frequently occurring adjacent pairs.

Let's build the idea manually

Imagine these training words:

play, player, played, playing, replay

Initially, we might represent words using individual characters:

Word: playing

p

l

a

y

i

n

g

Repeated adjacent-pair merges

play

i

n

g

play

ing

Illustrative possible merge progression. Which merges are actually learned, and in which order, depends on corpus pair frequencies and the chosen algorithm.

Why might the token play be useful?

Because it appears in several related words.

Instead of storing a separate embedding for every possible inflected form, the model can reuse subword representations.

However, BPE is not a morphological analyzer. It merges frequent symbol pairs, not necessarily meaningful prefixes, roots or suffixes.

For example, it may split a word at a linguistically unnatural boundary if that's what its learned merges produce.

The BPE algorithm

  1. Represent training words using initial symbols, usually characters or bytes.
  2. Count adjacent symbol pairs across the training corpus.
  3. Choose a frequently occurring pair and merge it into one symbol.
  4. Recalculate pair frequencies after the merge.
  5. Repeat until the desired merge budget or vocabulary size is reached.

Each merge adds another symbol that can be reused in tokenization.

Implement a small BPE trainer in Python

Let's make a simplified word-boundary-aware BPE implementation from scratch. We'll use word counts and an explicit end-of-word marker.

Python
from collections import Counter

# Training vocabulary with frequencies
training_words = Counter({
    "play": 8,
    "playing": 6,
    "player": 5,
    "played": 4,
    "replay": 3
})

# Start with characters plus an end-of-word symbol
pieces = {
    tuple(word) + ("</w>",): freq
    for word, freq in training_words.items()
}

def count_pairs(vocabulary):
    pair_counts = Counter()

    for symbols, frequency in vocabulary.items():
        for a, b in zip(symbols, symbols[1:]):
            pair_counts[(a, b)] += frequency

    return pair_counts


def merge_pair(symbols, pair):
    result = []
    i = 0

    while i < len(symbols):
        if (
            i + 1 < len(symbols)
            and (symbols[i], symbols[i + 1]) == pair
        ):
            result.append(symbols[i] + symbols[i + 1])
            i += 2
        else:
            result.append(symbols[i])
            i += 1

    return tuple(result)


merges = []

for _ in range(12):
    pair_counts = count_pairs(pieces)

    if not pair_counts:
        break

    # Most frequent adjacent pair
    best_pair = pair_counts.most_common(1)[0][0]

    merges.append(best_pair)

    pieces = {
        merge_pair(symbols, best_pair): freq
        for symbols, freq in pieces.items()
    }


def bpe_encode(word):
    symbols = tuple(word) + ("</w>",)

    # Apply the learned merges in training order
    for pair in merges:
        symbols = merge_pair(symbols, pair)

    # Hide our educational end-of-word marker
    return [
        s.replace("</w>", "")
        for s in symbols
        if s != "</w>"
    ]


print("First learned merges:", merges[:5])
print("playing:", bpe_encode("playing"))
print("replaying:", bpe_encode("replaying"))

There is something important happening here.

We have two separate processes:

  1. Tokenizer training: Learn useful merges from a corpus.

  2. Tokenizer inference: Apply those learned merges to new text.

The tokenizer does not ordinarily relearn its vocabulary every time the neural network receives a batch.

Once established, its vocabulary and merge rules remain fixed during normal model training and inference.

This is an educational BPE implementation, not a full production byte-level tokenizer. It also assumes the input characters belong to its supported alphabet.

7. BPE versus WordPiece versus Unigram

These are three widely used subword approaches.

They share the motivation of reducing vocabulary sparsity while keeping sequences reasonably short.

But their learning strategies differ.

Algorithm

Central idea

Common association

BPE

Repeatedly merge frequent adjacent symbols

GPT-2-style byte-level BPE

WordPiece

Learn a vocabulary using merge decisions guided by a vocabulary-scoring criterion

BERT-style tokenizers

Unigram

Start with candidate pieces, estimate their probabilities and remove less useful pieces

SentencePiece Unigram; T5 tokenizers

WordPiece

WordPiece can look similar to BPE when encoding.

For example, a WordPiece vocabulary might segment:

playing → play + ##ing

The ## convention indicates a piece that continues a word in certain WordPiece tokenizers.

However, WordPiece's vocabulary-learning strategy isn't simply identical to BPE's most-frequent-pair rule.

Unigram

Unigram takes a different approach.

It considers a vocabulary of possible subword pieces and estimates how likely those pieces are.

A word may have several possible segmentations. The tokenizer selects a likely segmentation based on its learned piece probabilities, and training can remove pieces that contribute little.

Byte-level BPE

An important modern variation begins with bytes rather than a fixed set of Unicode characters.

This enables the tokenizer to represent arbitrary UTF-8 text without relying on an unknown-word token for unfamiliar characters, provided the full byte alphabet is supported.

For example, emojis, multilingual scripts and uncommon symbols can be represented through byte sequences even when a convenient whole-token entry is unavailable.

The disadvantage is that unfamiliar text may require many tokens.

A subtle but important point

Tokenization strategy and Transformer architecture are separate design choices.

BPE does not require GPT, and WordPiece does not require BERT. They became associated with certain model families because of historical implementation choices.

Modern models may use different tokenizer implementations even when they share broadly similar neural architectures.

8. Sentence boundaries, special tokens and text reconstruction

We've focused on individual words and subwords. But in practice, a document can contain many sentences, paragraphs and other structures.

Consider:

Dr. Smith arrived at 8 p.m. He was late.

If we simply split on every period, we'd incorrectly break the text inside Dr. and p.m..

Sentence segmentation is itself an NLP problem.

A tokenizer also has to decide how to handle spaces, punctuation and other boundaries.

For example, depending on the tokenizer, a leading space may be incorporated into a token:

"hello" and " hello" may have different tokenizations.

This is one reason why modern tokenizers don't always produce intuitive word lists.

Encoding versus decoding

We need to distinguish two operations:

  • Encode: Raw text → Token IDs

  • Decode: Token IDs → Text

For a tokenizer intended for text generation, decoding should recover the intended text as faithfully as possible.

Our simple lowercase word tokenizer is not perfectly reversible. It has already discarded capitalization and some spacing information.

More sophisticated tokenizers preserve sufficient information about spaces and symbols to reconstruct text, subject to any normalization they apply.

Token offsets

For token-level NLP tasks such as named entity recognition, we may also need to know where each token came from in the original text.

For example:

"The bank approved the loan."

If we're labeling the phrase "the loan" as a span, preserving character offsets is useful for mapping model predictions back to the original document.

Token-to-character alignment becomes important when working with annotated datasets.

We'll return to it in our sequence-labeling lesson.

9. Batching tokenized sequences

Now we've reached another direct connection to our neural-network lessons.

Remember the batching problem?

Different sentences can produce different numbers of tokens.

But PyTorch tensors in a conventional batch need consistent dimensions.

Suppose we tokenize:

1 = real token, 0 = padding. This is a padding mask, not a causal-attention mask.

The padding mask prevents models from treating artificial padding positions as meaningful input information.

For token-level training objectives, padded targets also need to be excluded from the loss.

Let's implement batching in PyTorch

Using our stoi, vocab and encode_words functions from Section 4:

Python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

sentences = [
    "The bank approved the loan.",
    "The river bank."
]

encoded = [encode_words(s) for s in sentences]

max_length = max(len(s) for s in encoded)

pad_id = stoi["<PAD>"]

# Pad shorter sequences
batch = torch.tensor([
    s + [pad_id] * (max_length - len(s))
    for s in encoded
], dtype=torch.long)

# True for real tokens
attention_mask = batch != pad_id

# Embedding layer
embedding = nn.Embedding(
    num_embeddings=len(vocab),
    embedding_dim=8,
    padding_idx=pad_id
)

vectors = embedding(batch)

print("Token IDs:", batch.shape)
print("Mask:", attention_mask.shape)
print("Embeddings:", vectors.shape)

# Token IDs: torch.Size([2, 8])
# Mask: torch.Size([2, 8])
# Embeddings: torch.Size([2, 8, 8])

Here's what happened:

Token IDs

(B,T)=(2,8)(B,T)=(2,8)

Embedding lookup

E∈RV×DE\in\mathbb R^{V\times D}

Embedded batch

(B,T,D)=(2,8,8)(B,T,D)=(2,8,8)

Now the text is ready for a neural model.

Our original MLP, RNN and Transformer concepts all fit back into the picture.

What about truncation?

If a sequence exceeds the model's allowed input length, a pipeline may truncate it or divide it into chunks.

But truncation can remove crucial information.

Imagine classifying an argument where the conclusion appears at the very end of a long paragraph. Truncating the final sentence may completely change what the model can infer.

So padding and truncation aren't merely technical conveniences. They can affect performance and correctness.

10. How tokenization affects model behavior

Let's summarize a few important consequences.

Vocabulary size versus sequence length

Larger vocabulary

Can represent frequent words and phrases with fewer tokens, but requires more vocabulary parameters.

Smaller vocabulary

Can reuse smaller pieces, but may produce longer sequences.

Longer sequences increase memory and computation for sequence models, especially full-attention Transformers.

Larger vocabularies increase the embedding table and often the output vocabulary projection.

There isn't one universally optimal vocabulary size.

Language coverage

A tokenizer trained mainly on one language may represent another language inefficiently.

For instance, familiar English words may receive compact tokenizations while some words from less-represented languages are split into many smaller units.

This can affect:

  • Effective context length.

  • Training and inference cost.

  • How much linguistic information each token represents.

  • Downstream performance.

Tokenization is not semantic understanding

Remember our word "bank"?

A tokenizer might produce the same token ID in:

"The bank approved the loan."

"The fisherman sat on the bank."

That is completely fine.

The tokenizer isn't responsible for deciding which meaning of "bank" is intended.

The contextual model is responsible for learning representations that reflect the surrounding information.

"bank" → Token ID 5 → Initial embedding

Financial context

loan, approved

River context

fisherman, river

Different contextual representations can emerge

This connects directly to our Transformer encoder lesson from Deep Learning Architectures.

The same initial embedding can be transformed differently depending on context.

11. A practical NLP pipeline: What should we actually do?

Before training a text classifier, a sound workflow is:

  1. Inspect the raw corpus and identify languages, encodings, text fields and annotation format.
  2. Split the data into training, validation and test sets using a strategy appropriate to the task, avoiding leakage.
  3. Choose preprocessing that preserves the information the task needs.
  4. Choose or train a tokenizer. If learning a new tokenizer for a supervised experiment, learn it from permitted training data, not from held-out test text.
  5. Build or use a fixed vocabulary and transform text into token IDs.
  6. Construct batches, masks and target labels or spans.
  7. Feed token IDs through embeddings and the model; calculate the appropriate loss.
  8. Keep the tokenizer configuration consistent during evaluation and deployment.

For a pretrained Transformer, most of the tokenizer decisions have already been made. We normally load the tokenizer paired with the model checkpoint.

For a model trained from scratch, tokenizer choice is part of the modeling design.

One important qualification: using a tokenizer from existing pretraining is not automatically evaluation leakage. Leakage concerns whether information from evaluation examples or labels improperly influences the experimental procedure. We need to consider the dataset and evaluation protocol.

12. Understanding check

Suppose we have a word-level tokenizer with a vocabulary of 20,000 words.

During inference, it encounters the word unhelpfulness, which isn't in the vocabulary.

Why might a subword tokenizer handle this better?

Answer and explanation

B. A subword tokenizer can represent an unfamiliar word with smaller pieces it already knows. The exact segmentation depends on its vocabulary and algorithm.

13. Final mental model

1. Text processing

Decide how to handle raw text, Unicode, capitalization, punctuation and other formatting.

2. Tokenization

Divide text into units: words, subwords, characters or byte-based pieces.

3. Vocabulary

Assign a unique integer ID to every supported token.

4. Subword algorithms

BPE learns merges, WordPiece learns a scored vocabulary, and Unigram learns a probabilistic subword vocabulary.

5. Batching

Pad or otherwise organize variable-length sequences, construct appropriate masks and handle length limits.

6. Embeddings

Map token IDs into learned numerical vectors that a neural network can process.

7. Contextualization

The neural model transforms those vectors using surrounding information. Tokenization itself doesn't resolve semantic ambiguity.

The discovery that leads to Lesson 3

We've learned to transform text into a sequence of token IDs.

But that still leaves a critical question:

How should we represent an entire document for classification or retrieval?

Suppose we want to classify:

"The bank approved the loan."

as a financial statement.

Do we need a complicated Transformer?

Not necessarily.

We could first represent the document using which words appear and how frequently they occur.

That leads us to the earliest practical numerical text representations:

Document tokens

Bag-of-Words

Counts

N-grams

Local order

TF-IDF

Term importance

Sparse numerical document vector → ML model

And then another question emerges: if some words like "the" appear everywhere, should they really contribute as much as more informative words like "approved" or "loan"?

That is precisely the limitation that motivates TF-IDF.

Next: Lesson 3 — Bag-of-Words, N-grams and TF-IDF. We'll build our first classical NLP document classifier from scratch, visualize document vectors and discover how text can be represented mathematically without a neural network at all.

1. Bag-of-Words — The simplest document representation

Consider our original sentence:

"The bank approved the loan."

We can create a vocabulary containing:

the, bank, approved, loan, river, flooded

Instead of representing the document as a sequence, let's count each vocabulary word.

Bag-of-Words transformation

the

bank

approved

the

loan

the

bank

approved

loan

river

flooded

2
1
1
1
0
0

The document becomes a fixed-length numerical vector.

x=[2,1,1,1,0,0]x=[2,1,1,1,0,0]

This is a Bag-of-Words (BoW) representation.

Its defining characteristic:

We count which vocabulary words appear, but we discard their original positions and order.

Why call it a "bag"?

Because it treats the document like an unordered collection of words.

Let's compare:

"The dog chased the cat."

"The cat chased the dog."

Both have the same Bag-of-Words counts:

Word

Sentence 1

Sentence 2

the

2

2

dog

1

1

chased

1

1

cat

1

1

Their vectors are identical.

We already know why that's a limitation: the grammatical roles differ.

But BoW can still be extremely effective for tasks where word presence is highly predictive.

For example, documents containing mortgage, interest, loan and investment may be more likely to concern finance.

Build BoW from scratch

Python
from collections import Counter
import re

documents = [
    "the bank approved the loan",
    "the bank offered the loan",
    "the river bank flooded",
    "the river flooded the path"
]

def tokenize(text):
    return re.findall(r"[a-z]+", text.lower())

# Vocabulary learned from our corpus
vocab = sorted({
    word
    for doc in documents
    for word in tokenize(doc)
})

def bow_vector(text, vocab):
    counts = Counter(tokenize(text))
    return [counts[word] for word in vocab]

for doc in documents:
    print(doc)
    print(bow_vector(doc, vocab))

print("Vocabulary:", vocab)

Note that this is not a neural network yet. We're only constructing numerical input features.

2. The document-term matrix

If we represent many documents using the same vocabulary, we can stack their feature vectors into one matrix.

Suppose we focus on six words.

Document-term matrix

Terms such as "offered" and "path" are omitted from this illustrative six-column view. A full BoW representation includes every vocabulary column.

Mathematically:

X∈RN×V\boxed{X\in\mathbb R^{N\times V}}

Where:

  • NN = number of documents.

  • VV = vocabulary size.

  • XijX_{ij} = count of vocabulary term jj in document ii.

If we have 10,000 documents and 50,000 vocabulary terms:

X.shape=(10,000,50,000)X.shape=(10{,}000,50{,}000)

That is 500 million possible entries.

But most documents contain only a tiny fraction of the vocabulary.

So most entries are zero.

Sparse representations

A sparse matrix stores primarily the nonzero entries and their positions, rather than explicitly storing every zero.

Dense versus sparse storage

Dense

Stores all entries

[2, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, …]

Sparse

Stores nonzero entries

(0:2), (1:1), (2:1), (3:1)

This matters because classical NLP frequently uses very high-dimensional, extremely sparse feature vectors.

scikit-learn implementation

Python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer

vectorizer = CountVectorizer()

X = vectorizer.fit_transform(documents)

print("Shape:", X.shape)
print("Vocabulary:", vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())
print("Sparse format:", X.getformat())

# Convert to dense only for this small demonstration
print(X.toarray())

CountVectorizer constructs the vocabulary and produces a sparse document-term matrix.

The matrix is ready to be passed to an ML classifier.

But we're about to discover a problem.

3. The first limitation: Bag-of-Words forgets order

Consider:

"The movie is good."

"The movie is not good."

A BoW representation captures the presence of not, but doesn't represent the relationship or ordering of not and good.

It can potentially learn that the token not correlates with negative sentiment, but it cannot explicitly distinguish arbitrary word-order changes.

How could we fix this without building an RNN or Transformer?

Instead of counting individual words, count sequences of neighboring words.

That leads naturally to n-grams.

4. N-grams — Preserving local word order

An n-gram is a contiguous sequence of nn tokens.

For the sentence:

the cat chased the dog

N-gram explorer

thecatchasedthedog
Position2-gram feature
1the cat
2cat chased
3chased the
4the dog

Why are bigrams useful?

Compare:

  • not good

  • good not

Their individual unigram counts are identical.

Their bigram features differ.

For sentiment classification, the bigram not good may be more informative than the individual word good.

Similarly:

  • New York

  • York New

have different local word-order patterns.

But n-grams introduce another problem

As nn increases, the number of possible token combinations grows rapidly.

With vocabulary size VV:

  • Possible unigrams: VV

  • Possible bigrams: V2V^2

  • Possible trigrams: V3V^3

Not all of those combinations occur in real data, but the potential feature space is enormous.

That creates sparsity.

Many valid n-grams appear rarely or never in the training data.

Generate n-grams with Python

Python
def ngrams(tokens, n):
    return [
        tuple(tokens[i:i+n])
        for i in range(len(tokens)-n+1)
    ]

sentence = "the cat chased the dog"
tokens = tokenize(sentence)

print("Unigrams:", ngrams(tokens, 1))
print("Bigrams:", ngrams(tokens, 2))
print("Trigrams:", ngrams(tokens, 3))

scikit-learn: Combine unigrams and bigrams

Python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer

vectorizer = CountVectorizer(
    ngram_range=(1, 2)
)

X = vectorizer.fit_transform([
    "the movie is good",
    "the movie is not good",
    "the food is not good"
])

print(vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())
print(X.shape)

ngram_range=(1,2) tells the vectorizer to include both single-word and two-word features.

This is often a powerful classical NLP baseline.

But we still haven't addressed another problem.

Why should extremely common words such as "the" contribute so much to document representations?

That motivates TF-IDF.

5. TF-IDF — Not every word is equally informative

Let's return to our four-document corpus:

D1: the bank approved the loan

D2: the bank offered the loan

D3: the river bank flooded

D4: the river flooded the path

Notice something interesting.

The word the occurs in every document.

The word approved occurs in only one.

If we're trying to identify which document discusses loan approval, approved is potentially more discriminative than the.

This motivates Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF).

The central idea:

A term should receive more weight when it occurs in a document but less weight when it is common across many documents.

We accomplish this by combining two values.

Part A — Term Frequency (TF)

Term frequency measures how often a term occurs in a particular document.

For our simplest version, we'll use the raw count:

TF⁡(t,d)=count⁡(t,d)\boxed{\operatorname{TF}(t,d)=\operatorname{count}(t,d)}

In D1:

  • the appears twice → TF = 2.

  • bank appears once → TF = 1.

  • approved appears once → TF = 1.

This alone is just Bag-of-Words.

Part B — Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)

Now we introduce information from the entire training corpus.

Let NN be the total number of documents, and df⁡(t)\operatorname{df}(t) be the number of documents containing term tt.

A simple IDF formula is:

IDF⁡(t)=ln⁡(Ndf⁡(t))\boxed{\operatorname{IDF}(t)=\ln\left(\frac{N}{\operatorname{df}(t)}\right)}

Here N=4N=4.

Term

Look at the pattern: the more documents contain a term, the lower its IDF becomes.

Inverse document frequency

Calculated using IDF = ln(4 / document frequency) for our four-document corpus. Larger values mean greater rarity across these documents.

Part C — Multiply them

TFIDF⁡(t,d)=TF⁡(t,d)×IDF⁡(t)\boxed{\operatorname{TFIDF}(t,d)=\operatorname{TF}(t,d)\times\operatorname{IDF}(t)}

For D1:

In the same six-column order as the count matrix (the, bank, approved, loan, river, flooded), the simplified TF-IDF vector is:

xD1=[0, 0.288, 1.386, 0.693, 0, 0]x_{\text{D1}}=[0,\ 0.288,\ 1.386,\ 0.693,\ 0,\ 0]

Suddenly, the most common word has zero weight, while approved receives a much larger weight.

TF-IDF is still a fixed-dimensional document vector, but its entries now reflect both term frequency and corpus-wide rarity.

Interactive TF-IDF explorer

Change the document and term to see how each value is calculated.

thebankapprovedtheloan

Notice that a rare word still receives a weight of zero in a document where it doesn't occur.

Try selecting the and then approved in D1.

Even though the appears twice, its simplified IDF is zero because every document contains it.

approved appears only once, but its IDF is high.

Important: TF-IDF has several variants

The formula above is a useful conceptual starting point, but production implementations often add smoothing, normalize vectors, or modify term frequency.

For example, scikit-learn's default TfidfVectorizer uses:

IDF⁡sklearn(t)=ln⁡(1+N1+df⁡(t))+1\operatorname{IDF}_{\text{sklearn}}(t)= \ln\left(\frac{1+N}{1+\operatorname{df}(t)}\right)+1

By default, it also applies L2 normalization to document vectors.

Consequently, its output values will not exactly match our simplified table, and even words appearing in every document retain positive IDF.

The intuition remains the same: more widely distributed terms receive less relative emphasis.

6. Implement TF-IDF from scratch

Let's calculate the simplified version ourselves first.

Python
import math
from collections import Counter

documents = [
    "the bank approved the loan",
    "the bank offered the loan",
    "the river bank flooded",
    "the river flooded the path"
]

tokenized = [tokenize(doc) for doc in documents]

vocab = sorted({
    term for doc in tokenized for term in doc
})

N = len(documents)

# Count how many documents contain each term
df = {
    term: sum(term in set(doc) for doc in tokenized)
    for term in vocab
}

idf = {
    term: math.log(N / df[term])
    for term in vocab
}

def tfidf_vector(tokens):
    counts = Counter(tokens)

    return [
        counts[term] * idf[term]
        for term in vocab
    ]


for tokens in tokenized:
    print(tokens)
    print([round(x, 3) for x in tfidf_vector(tokens)])

print("IDF('the'):", idf["the"])
print("IDF('approved'):", round(idf["approved"], 3))

And now the practical scikit-learn implementation:

Python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer

vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer()

X = vectorizer.fit_transform(documents)

print("Matrix shape:", X.shape)
print("Vocabulary:", vectorizer.get_feature_names_out())

# Inspect one document's nonzero features
features = vectorizer.get_feature_names_out()
row = X[0].toarray().ravel()

for term, weight in zip(features, row):
    if weight > 0:
        print(term, round(weight, 3))

We didn't need a neural network for any of this.

The vectorizer computes document representations from counts and corpus statistics.

But we can now feed those vectors to a model that learns to classify documents.

7. From TF-IDF vectors to a document classifier

Now we're ready to connect text representations to machine learning.

Our goal is to classify documents into:

  • Finance

  • Environment

Let's represent a document using TF-IDF:

x=[x1,x2,…,xV]x=[x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_V]

Each xix_i is the TF-IDF weight of one vocabulary feature.

Now remember our original neuron:

z=w1x1+w2x2+⋯+wVxV+bz=w_1x_1+w_2x_2+\cdots+w_Vx_V+b

We can use the exact same operation!

Raw document

"The bank approved a loan."

Tokenization → TF-IDF feature vector

Linear model

z=wTx+bz=w^Tx+b

One learned coefficient for each vocabulary feature

Sigmoid

p=σ(z)p=\sigma(z)

Probability of the finance class

This is logistic regression, a classical linear classification model.

Notice the separation:

  • TF-IDF features: Calculated from documents using fixed statistical rules.

  • Model weights: Learned using labeled examples.

  • Prediction: A linear score transformed into a probability.

  • Training: Optimize a classification objective, commonly log loss.

The TF-IDF vectorizer does not learn which words indicate finance. The classifier learns that relationship.

For example, it might learn a positive coefficient for mortgage and a negative coefficient for forest, assuming we're predicting the finance class.

Train a complete classical NLP classifier

The code below is self-contained and compares count-based features against TF-IDF.

Python
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import (
    CountVectorizer, TfidfVectorizer
)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score, classification_report
)

finance = [
    "The bank approved a personal loan",
    "The borrower paid interest on the mortgage",
    "The credit union opened a savings account",
    "The lender rejected the loan application",
    "The bank reduced the interest rate",
    "The customer deposited money into the account",
    "The financial firm issued new bonds",
    "The mortgage payment was due today",
    "The bank processed a card payment",
    "The borrower requested a larger loan",
    "The investor purchased company shares",
    "The loan officer checked the credit report"
]

environment = [
    "The river flooded the nearby village",
    "The fisherman waited beside the river bank",
    "The forest animals moved toward the lake",
    "The heavy rain caused water levels to rise",
    "The stream flowed through the valley",
    "The river overflowed after the storm",
    "The birds nested along the river",
    "The muddy path followed the river bend",
    "The mountain lake was covered in fog",
    "The wetland was home to rare insects",
    "The rain soaked the forest floor",
    "The river water reached the old bridge"
]

texts = finance + environment

labels = (
    ["finance"] * len(finance)
    + ["environment"] * len(environment)
)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    texts,
    labels,
    test_size=0.25,
    random_state=42,
    stratify=labels
)

# Model A: Bag-of-Words with unigrams and bigrams
bow_model = Pipeline([
    ("features", CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2))),
    ("classifier", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
])

# Model B: TF-IDF with unigrams and bigrams
tfidf_model = Pipeline([
    ("features", TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2))),
    ("classifier", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
])

for name, model in [
    ("Bag-of-Words", bow_model),
    ("TF-IDF", tfidf_model)
]:
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    predictions = model.predict(X_test)

    print(f"\n{name}")
    print("Accuracy:", accuracy_score(y_test, predictions))
    print(classification_report(
        y_test, predictions, zero_division=0
    ))

We're not assuming TF-IDF must outperform raw counts. That depends on the data, algorithm and task.

This tiny dataset is just for understanding the complete pipeline. Six held-out examples are far too few for reliable performance conclusions.

Why use a Pipeline?

This is important for proper evaluation.

The vectorizer must learn its vocabulary and IDF statistics from the training data, not the held-out test set.

When we call:

Python
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

the Pipeline fits both the vectorizer and classifier using training data.

During:

Python
model.predict(X_test)

it applies the already-fitted vectorizer to the test documents.

This prevents us from accidentally fitting corpus-level TF-IDF statistics on held-out test data.

What did the classifier learn?

Let's inspect its coefficients.

Python
import numpy as np

features = tfidf_model.named_steps[
    "features"
].get_feature_names_out()

classifier = tfidf_model.named_steps["classifier"]

# For binary logistic regression, coefficients
# are for classifier.classes_[1].
positive_class = classifier.classes_[1]

weights = classifier.coef_[0]
order = np.argsort(weights)

print("Positive class:", positive_class)

print("\nHighest positive coefficients:")
for i in order[-8:][::-1]:
    print(features[i], round(weights[i], 3))

print("\nHighest negative coefficients:")
for i in order[:8]:
    print(features[i], round(weights[i], 3))

This gives us something valuable: a direct connection between learned model weights and vocabulary features.

The model might associate financial terminology with finance and river-related terminology with environment.

However, correlated words and small datasets can make individual coefficients unstable. A coefficient is not automatically proof of a causal linguistic relationship.

8. TF-IDF is also useful for document similarity

Our feature vectors don't have to be used only for classification.

Imagine we have a document:

"The bank approved the loan."

And want to retrieve related documents.

We can compute similarity between their TF-IDF vectors.

A common measure is cosine similarity:

cos⁡(x,y)=xTy∥x∥∥y∥\boxed{ \cos(x,y)= \frac{x^Ty}{\|x\|\|y\|} }

It measures the angle between two nonzero vectors rather than their raw magnitudes.

Conceptual 2D illustration. Real TF-IDF vectors typically have hundreds or thousands of dimensions.

Documents with similar weighted vocabulary features tend to point in similar directions.

In scikit-learn, default TF-IDF vectors are L2-normalized, which makes their dot product equal to their cosine similarity.

Python
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

documents = [
    "the bank approved the loan",
    "the bank offered the loan",
    "the river bank flooded",
    "the river flooded the path"
]

vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer()
X = vectorizer.fit_transform(documents)

similarity = cosine_similarity(X)

print(similarity.round(3))

You should see that documents sharing terms like bank and loan have some lexical similarity.

But we have discovered a limitation.

Can TF-IDF recognize synonyms?

Consider:

"The physician examined the patient."

"The doctor checked the patient."

Humans recognize a strong semantic relationship.

A basic word-level TF-IDF representation treats physician and doctor as different features.

Unless the documents share other vocabulary, their similarity may be low despite their related meanings.

TF-IDF is excellent at capturing lexical overlap. It does not inherently understand that two different words can express similar concepts.

That's part of the motivation for the distributional word representations we'll study later.

9. What can classical text representations learn—and what can't they?

We can now compare our three approaches.

Feature

Bag-of-Words

Word n-grams

TF-IDF

Tracks word frequency

Yes

Yes, for selected n-grams

Yes, with reweighting

Preserves word order

No

No

Yes

No

Usually

Yes

Yes

An important distinction: TF-IDF is a weighting scheme, not a separate solution to word order. We can apply TF-IDF to individual words, n-grams or other discrete features.

Three limitations worth remembering

1. Lexical mismatch

"Doctor" and "physician" can be semantically similar while having different feature positions.

2. Limited compositional understanding

N-grams capture some local order, but complex relationships spanning distant tokens remain difficult to represent efficiently.

3. Context-dependent meaning

The TF-IDF feature for "bank" doesn't change its meaning depending on whether the sentence concerns a river or a loan. A classifier can exploit nearby words and n-grams, but the representation itself isn't contextualized.

These limitations don't make classical NLP obsolete.

Sparse lexical representations remain valuable for text classification, search, retrieval, interpretability and strong baselines.

Later, when we study information retrieval, we'll build on TF-IDF to understand BM25, and then compare lexical retrieval with embedding-based semantic search.

10. Connect everything to our original neural network

This is the part I want you to retain from our earlier volumes.

Raw document

Tokenizer → Vocabulary terms

BoW

N-grams

TF-IDF

Fixed-dimensional sparse feature vector x

Learned classifier

z=wTx+bz=w^Tx+b

Prediction → Classification loss

Optimize classifier parameters

Compared with a Transformer, a major difference is where representation learning happens.

In a classical TF-IDF + logistic regression pipeline, the numerical text representation is calculated using fixed rules and corpus statistics, while the classifier learns feature coefficients.

In a Transformer, token embeddings and contextual representations are learned through the neural network's trainable parameters.

Both approaches ultimately produce predictions and optimize a task-specific objective.

11. Understanding check

Consider a corpus where the word the occurs in every document, but mortgage occurs in only a few.

Why might TF-IDF give "mortgage" a higher weight than "the"?

Answer and explanation

B. A rarer term receives a higher inverse document frequency. Its total weight still depends on its frequency in the selected document.

12. Final mental model

1. Bag-of-Words represents documents using word counts.

It produces fixed-dimensional vectors but discards word order.

2. N-grams preserve local order.

They capture adjacent token combinations, at the cost of larger and sparser feature spaces.

3. TF-IDF weights terms according to frequency and rarity.

Terms common across the corpus receive less relative emphasis than more document-specific terms.

4. Document representations are usually sparse.

Most documents contain only a small subset of all vocabulary features.

5. Classical ML models can learn directly from these vectors.

A linear classifier learns feature weights using labeled documents.

6. These methods are lexical, not inherently contextual.

They don't automatically understand synonyms, distant dependencies or a word's changing meaning.

The discovery that leads to Lesson 4

We've learned how to count words and n-grams across documents.

But what if we use those same counts for something more ambitious?

Instead of predicting a document's category, could we predict the next word?

Suppose our corpus contains:

"The cat sleeps."

"The dog runs."

"The cat runs."

We can calculate:

P(cat∣the)=23P(\text{cat}\mid\text{the})=\frac{2}{3}
P(dog∣the)=13P(\text{dog}\mid\text{the})=\frac{1}{3}

We're no longer merely representing text. We're estimating probabilities of what comes next.

Count word sequences

Estimate conditional probabilities

Predict the next word

Repeat → Generate text

But another problem immediately appears.

What if we've never seen a particular word combination before? Should its probability always be zero?

And how can we assign a probability to an entire sentence?

That brings us to Lesson 4 — Statistical Language Modeling, where we'll study the probability chain rule, n-gram language models, Markov assumptions, smoothing, entropy, cross-entropy and perplexity.

This is one of the most important conceptual bridges to modern LLMs: we'll discover that next-token prediction existed long before Transformers, and see exactly which limitations neural language models were designed to overcome.

Conditional probability · N-gram language models · Markov assumptions · Smoothing · Cross-entropy · Perplexity

In Lesson 3, we learned to count words and n-grams and turn documents into numerical vectors.

Now we're going to use those same counts to do something much more interesting:

Build a model that predicts the next word and can generate an entire sentence.

And here's the connection to Deep Learning Architectures: the fundamental objective behind GPT-style next-token prediction existed long before Transformers.

The main difference is how the next-token probabilities are estimated.

1. Our case study: A tiny language model

Imagine our complete training corpus contains just three sentences:

S1

The cat sleeps.

S2

The dog runs.

S3

The cat runs.
For our numerical example, we'll lowercase the text, omit periods, and add explicit beginning/end markers.

Suppose the model has read:

"the ..."

What comes next?

We can simply count:

  • the cat appears twice.

  • the dog appears once.

So:

P(cat∣the)=23P(\text{cat}\mid\text{the})=\frac23
P(dog∣the)=13P(\text{dog}\mid\text{the})=\frac13

Next-word distribution after "the"

cat

66.7%

dog

33.3%

We've just built the simplest kind of statistical language model.

It estimates a probability distribution over the next word, based on previously observed words.

Let's formalize this.

2. What exactly is a language model?

A language model estimates the probability of a sequence of tokens:

P(w1,w2,…,wT)\boxed{P(w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_T)}

That means it can assign different probabilities to different sequences.

For example:

"the cat sleeps"

might have a higher probability than:

"sleeps cat the"

under a model trained on ordinary English.

A language model is not inherently a chatbot, a Transformer or even a neural network.

It's a model of token sequence probabilities.

The probability chain rule

Remember conditional probabilities?

We can always decompose the joint probability of a sequence into conditional probabilities:

P(w1,…,wT)=∏t=1TP(wt∣w1,…,wt−1)\boxed{ P(w_1,\ldots,w_T)= \prod_{t=1}^{T}P(w_t\mid w_1,\ldots,w_{t-1}) }

For a three-word sentence:

P(the cat sleeps)=P(the)P(cat∣the)P(sleeps∣the cat)P(\text{the cat sleeps}) = P(\text{the}) P(\text{cat}\mid\text{the}) P(\text{sleeps}\mid\text{the cat})

For a complete sentence model, we also commonly include beginning/end markers.

This factorization is exact. We haven't made any simplifying assumptions yet.

The challenge is estimating probabilities conditioned on potentially very long histories.

And that leads directly to n-gram language models.

3. The Markov assumption — Limit how far back we look

Imagine estimating:

P(wt∣w1,…,wt−1)P(w_t\mid w_1,\ldots,w_{t-1})

For a sentence containing 100 words, we'd condition on up to 99 preceding words.

How many examples of that exact 99-word context would we expect to find in a limited training corpus?

Probably very few, if any.

We need a simplification.

Bigram language model

A bigram model assumes that the next word depends only on the previous word:

P(wt∣w<t)≈P(wt∣wt−1)\boxed{P(w_t\mid w_{<t})\approx P(w_t\mid w_{t-1})}

Trigram language model

A trigram model looks at the previous two words:

P(wt∣w<t)≈P(wt∣wt−2,wt−1)\boxed{P(w_t\mid w_{<t})\approx P(w_t\mid w_{t-2},w_{t-1})}

More generally, an n-gram language model conditions on the preceding n−1n-1 tokens.

How much context can the model use?

Target: sleeps

cat

Estimated conditional probability: P(sleeps | cat)

A larger n can use more local context, but requires observing more specific word combinations.

Here's the important trade-off:

Model

Context used

Main trade-off

Unigram

No previous words

Simple, but ignores order

Bigram

Previous 1 word

Captures local transitions

Trigram

Previous 2 words

More context, sparser observations

5-gram

Previous 4 words

More specific, often many unseen contexts

A bigger context is potentially more informative, but the counts become less reliable when exact combinations are rare.

The Markov assumption makes language modeling tractable by deliberately forgetting most of the history.

4. Estimate bigram probabilities from counts

Let's return to our three-sentence corpus.

We'll include explicit sequence boundaries:

BOS

the

cat

sleeps

EOS

BOS

the

dog

runs

EOS

BOS

the

cat

runs

EOS

BOS marks the beginning and EOS marks the end. These markers allow the model to learn when sentences start and finish.

For a bigram model, we count pairs and normalize by the number of times the conditioning word occurs as a predecessor:

P(wt∣wt−1)=C(wt−1,wt)C(wt−1)\boxed{ P(w_t\mid w_{t-1})= \frac{C(w_{t-1},w_t)} {C(w_{t-1})} }

Here C(wt−1)C(w_{t-1}) counts observed outgoing transitions from that context. This gives us a valid probability distribution over the possible next tokens.

These are maximum-likelihood estimates (MLE): choose the probabilities that maximize the likelihood of the observed transitions, without imposing smoothing or other constraints.
