Chapter 9

Summary and interview questions

Complete revision summary + 6 carefully selected, real-world interview questions

In Deep Learning Basics, we learned how neural networks learn.

In Deep Learning Architectures, we learned how different architectures process different types of information.

Natural Language Processing asks a more fundamental question:

How can a machine turn human language into something it can represent, understand, search, classify and generate?

Language creates problems that ordinary numerical or image data don't necessarily have.

The same idea can be expressed using different words. The same word can carry different meanings. Meaning depends on context, grammatical structure, intention and sometimes knowledge that isn't explicitly stated.

Our NLP course followed the development from simple statistical representations to contextual language models, information retrieval, structured prediction and robust evaluation.

The central idea connecting everything is:

NLP is about choosing representations that preserve the linguistic information needed for a task—and evaluating whether those representations generalize beyond the examples used to develop them.

Part I — The complete conceptual summary

What makes natural language difficult?

Consider these three sentences: - "The film was absolutely fantastic." - "I really enjoyed watching that movie." - "The movie was not bad at all." They express broadly positive sentiment but use different words and constructions.

Now consider: - "The movie was good." - "The movie was not good." These sentences share almost every word but have opposite sentiment.

This exposes two fundamental challenges.

Lexical variation: Different words and expressions can communicate similar meanings.

Compositional meaning: Small changes in word order, structure or context can significantly change the meaning.

Language also includes ambiguity.

For example: "I went to the bank."

Does bank refer to a financial institution or the side of a river?

Without context, both interpretations are possible.

And language often requires relationships beyond individual words.

Consider: "The experiment produced a statistically significant improvement, although the result was not replicated on the second dataset."

A useful NLP representation must capture not just the positive phrase "significant improvement," but also the qualifying information that follows.

This leads to an important distinction:

Recognizing words isn't the same as representing what those words mean together.

NLP systems need increasingly sophisticated representations because linguistic meaning isn't simply the sum of individual word meanings.

Tokenization — How text becomes model input

A neural network doesn't directly process written text as human readers do.

First, we convert text into tokens.

A token is a unit selected by a tokenization procedure. It might represent a whole word, a subword fragment, a character or a byte-level unit.

For example:

unbelievable

Depending on the tokenizer, it might become:

["un", "believ", "able"]

or a single token.

Each token is mapped to a vocabulary ID.

The model receives these IDs, which are then transformed into numerical representations. Why not simply split on spaces? Word-level tokenization has several problems.

Consider: - walk - walked - walking - walker A word-level vocabulary might store all four as unrelated entries.

It would also struggle with rare words, new technical terms, spelling variations and languages with complex morphology.

A completely character-level tokenizer avoids most unknown-word problems, but sequences become much longer.

Subword tokenization provides a useful compromise. Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) BPE begins with smaller units and repeatedly merges frequently occurring adjacent pairs.

For example, a simplified training process might learn that the sequence:

l + o

frequently occurs, so it merges them into:

lo

Later it may merge:

lo + w

into:

low.

The final vocabulary contains units of different lengths.

Common sequences may become single tokens, while unusual words are decomposed into smaller pieces.

The key advantage is that the vocabulary can represent many words without requiring a separate token for every possible word.

Byte-level BPE can additionally represent arbitrary text through its byte-level foundation, avoiding ordinary unknown-token problems. Why does tokenization matter beyond preprocessing? Tokenization influences: - Sequence length. - Computational cost. - Memory usage. - The efficiency of representing different languages. - How rare words and technical terms are processed. - How numerical strings, code and specialized terminology are segmented. Suppose two tokenizers represent the same document using 2,000 and 3,200 tokens respectively.

Even if the underlying words are identical, the second representation requires more token positions.

For a Transformer, that can increase computation and context-memory requirements.

But fewer tokens aren't automatically better: vocabulary size, segmentation quality and training compatibility also matter. An important distinction A tokenizer is not a semantic understanding system.

BPE merges frequently co-occurring character sequences. It doesn't inherently know that two words have similar meanings.

Tokenization decides the units the model receives.

Learning meaningful representations happens later.

This distinction becomes especially important when we study embeddings.

Bag-of-Words — Representing text by counting terms

One of the earliest useful NLP representations is Bag-of-Words (BoW).

The idea is simple:

Represent a document by which vocabulary terms appear and how often.

Suppose the vocabulary is:

["good", "bad", "movie"]

The sentence: "good movie good movie"

could become: x=[2,0,2]x=[2,0,2]

This is a numerical feature vector.

We can feed it into logistic regression, a linear classifier or another machine-learning model. Why does Bag-of-Words work surprisingly well? Many language tasks contain strong lexical signals.

For example, words such as "refund," "invoice" and "payment" may be useful for categorizing customer-support tickets.

BoW can exploit these signals efficiently.

It's also interpretable: we can inspect which words contribute to a prediction.

But its major limitation is that it generally ignores word order.

Compare: "The treatment improved survival."

and: "The treatment did not improve survival."

A simple word-count representation may capture most of the same content words and fail to adequately represent the negation relationship.

Likewise: "Dog bites man."

and: "Man bites dog."

have identical word counts but different meanings. N-grams partly address this Instead of representing only individual words, we can represent sequences of adjacent words.

For example, bigrams include: - "did not" - "not improve" - "improve survival" This can capture some local structure.

But larger n-gram vocabularies become sparse and expensive, and they still struggle to generalize between different phrasings.

BoW trades linguistic sophistication for simplicity, speed and lexical interpretability.

That trade-off remains useful in modern NLP.

TF-IDF — Not all words are equally informative

Bag-of-Words counts terms, but frequent words aren't necessarily useful for distinguishing documents.

Consider two terms: - "the" - "mitochondria" The word "the" appears in almost every English document.

"Mitochondria" is less frequent and may carry important information about a document's topic.

TF-IDF combines two ideas.

Term Frequency (TF): How often does the term appear in a particular document?

Inverse Document Frequency (IDF): How uncommon is the term across the document collection?

One common form is: TFIDF⁡(t,d)=TF⁡(t,d)log⁡NDF⁡(t)\boxed{ \operatorname{TFIDF}(t,d) = \operatorname{TF}(t,d) \log\frac{N}{\operatorname{DF}(t)} }

Where: - tt is a term. - dd is a document. - NN is the number of documents. - DF⁡(t)\operatorname{DF}(t) is the number of documents containing that term. Practical implementations often use smoothing and normalization. Intuition A word gets a relatively high weight when it occurs frequently in one document but isn't present across nearly every document.

This helps distinguish documents by their characteristic vocabulary.

TF-IDF vectors can be compared using cosine similarity, making the method useful for document retrieval and clustering. What TF-IDF does not know TF-IDF doesn't inherently know that:

"car" and "automobile"

are semantically related.

If the terms don't overlap, lexical similarity may be low even when the documents discuss the same topic.

But this lexical dependence can also be an advantage.

For exact technical identifiers, product codes, dates or specialized terminology, literal matching is often extremely valuable.

The lesson: Sparse representations can be excellent when exact lexical evidence matters, even if they don't deeply model meaning.

Statistical language modeling — Predicting words using context

Before neural language models became dominant, NLP systems often used n-gram language models.

The objective was to estimate the probability of a sequence: P(w1,w2,…,wT)P(w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_T)

Using the chain rule: P(w1,…,wT)=∏t=1TP(wt∣w<t)P(w_1,\ldots,w_T) = \prod_{t=1}^{T}P(w_t\mid w_{<t})

This decomposition is exact.

But estimating a probability conditioned on every previous word is difficult because the number of possible histories is enormous.

So n-gram models introduce a Markov approximation.

For a trigram model: P(wt∣w<t)≈P(wt∣wt−2,wt−1)\boxed{ P(w_t\mid w_{<t}) \approx P(w_t\mid w_{t-2},w_{t-1}) }

The model predicts the next word using only the previous two words. Example Suppose the corpus frequently contains: "The weather is beautiful."

Then the model may assign high probability to "beautiful" after "weather is."

But if it encounters: "The weather is spectacular."

and the combination was never observed, its estimated probability may be zero under naive count-based estimation.

This is the data sparsity problem. Smoothing and backoff We use smoothing to avoid assigning zero probability to plausible unseen events.

Backoff and interpolation combine higher-order n-gram estimates with lower-order models when evidence is sparse.

The intuition is:

If we haven't seen the exact three-word combination, we can still use evidence from shorter contexts.

But fixed n-gram models remain limited by their context length.

They can't naturally generalize semantic similarities as effectively as learned dense representations. Perplexity Language models are often evaluated using negative log-likelihood.

Perplexity is the exponential of the average negative log-likelihood: PPL=exp⁡(−1T∑t=1Tlog⁡P(wt∣w<t))\boxed{ \mathrm{PPL}= \exp\left( -\frac1T\sum_{t=1}^{T} \log P(w_t\mid w_{<t}) \right) }

Lower perplexity means the model assigns higher average probability to the evaluated sequence under the chosen tokenization and evaluation protocol.

A rough intuition is that perplexity reflects the model's effective uncertainty when predicting tokens.

But it isn't literally the number of choices the model considers. Why perplexity isn't everything A model with lower perplexity may not always be better at classification, reasoning, retrieval or instruction following.

It might predict fluent text well without producing factually correct answers.

Perplexity comparisons also require compatible tokenization and likelihood definitions. Directly comparing token-level perplexity across very different tokenizers can be misleading.

Perplexity measures predictive fit to text, not general intelligence.

This insight becomes even more important in our modern LLM lectures.

Distributional semantics — Learning meaning from context

Bag-of-Words captures lexical occurrence.

But how can we learn that words such as "doctor" and "physician" are related?

The answer begins with the distributional hypothesis:

Words used in similar contexts often have related meanings.

For example: "The doctor examined the patient."

"The physician examined the patient."

The words "doctor" and "physician" occur in similar linguistic environments.

If we collect enough examples, we can learn representations that capture some of those similarities. Co-occurrence matrices Imagine a matrix where each row represents a target word and each column represents a context word.

Each entry counts how frequently the two occur near each other.

Two target words with similar context patterns may have similar meanings.

But raw counts are distorted by very frequent words.

This motivates statistical association measures. Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) PMI measures how strongly a word-context pair co-occurs relative to what we'd expect if they were independent. PMI⁡(w,c)=log⁡P(w,c)P(w)P(c)\boxed{ \operatorname{PMI}(w,c) = \log\frac{P(w,c)}{P(w)P(c)} }

Positive PMI indicates that the pair occurs more often than expected under independence.

Negative PMI indicates less frequent co-occurrence than expected.

This gives a more informative representation than raw frequency alone.

But high PMI for rare pairs can be noisy, and co-occurrence statistics alone don't fully solve semantic understanding. Word2Vec Word2Vec learns dense word vectors using a predictive objective.

Instead of explicitly constructing a huge co-occurrence matrix, the model trains embeddings using context-prediction tasks.

Two common approaches are:

CBOW: Predict a target word from surrounding context words.

Skip-gram: Predict surrounding context words from a target word.

For example: "The scientist published a paper."

Skip-gram might use "scientist" to predict nearby words such as "the," "published" and "a."

Across a large corpus, words used in related contexts develop related embeddings. Negative sampling Predicting probabilities over an entire vocabulary at every training step can be expensive.

Negative sampling converts the objective into distinguishing observed word-context pairs from sampled noise pairs.

The model learns to score real pairs more highly than sampled negatives.

There is an important theoretical connection: Skip-gram with Negative Sampling can be related to factorizing a shifted PMI structure under particular assumptions.

This helps explain why predictive embeddings and statistical co-occurrence approaches are closely connected. What do embeddings really learn? A word embedding is a learned vector: ew∈Rde_w\in\mathbb R^d

The vector's dimensions usually don't have simple independent meanings such as "happiness" or "science."

Instead, meaning is represented through patterns across the dimensions and relationships between vectors.

Cosine similarity can help identify words with related representations.

But similarity must be interpreted carefully.

Words such as "good" and "bad" may have similar embeddings because they occur in similar contexts, even though their sentiment meanings contrast.

Distributional similarity isn't always the same as synonymy. The major limitation: One word, one vector Traditional Word2Vec assigns a word a relatively fixed representation.

Consider: "The bank approved the loan."

"The boat approached the river bank."

The word "bank" has different meanings, but ordinary static Word2Vec uses the same word vector for both occurrences.

This motivates contextual representations.

Transformer encoders generate token representations conditioned on the surrounding text.

The representation of "bank" can therefore differ between those two sentences.

This is the conceptual bridge from Word2Vec to BERT and modern contextual language models.

Structured NLP tasks — Predictions have relationships

Not every NLP task is whole-sentence classification.

Sometimes we need to make predictions at multiple related positions.

Consider Named Entity Recognition (NER): "Marie Curie worked in Paris."

We want to identify person and location spans.

A common tagging scheme is BIO: - B-PER: Beginning of a person entity. - I-PER: Continuation of a person entity. - B-LOC: Beginning of a location entity. - O: Outside a target entity. The output might be: Token Tag Marie B-PER Curie I-PER worked O in O Paris B-LOC

This is called sequence labeling. Why not classify each token independently? Because neighboring labels are related.

For example, an I-PER label generally shouldn't appear as the continuation of a location entity.

Independent token classifiers may assign locally plausible labels that form an invalid overall sequence.

A Conditional Random Field (CRF) can explicitly model dependencies between output labels. CRFs — Predict the best label sequence A linear-chain CRF assigns a score to an entire label sequence using emission and transition information.

A simplified scoring function is: S(x,y)=∑tEt(yt)+∑tAyt−1,yt\boxed{ S(x,y)= \sum_t E_t(y_t) + \sum_t A_{y_{t-1},y_t} }

Where: - Et(yt)E_t(y_t) is the score for assigning a label at position tt. - Ayt−1,ytA_{y_{t-1},y_t} is the learned transition score between neighboring labels. Instead of selecting the highest-scoring tag independently at every token, the model selects the highest-scoring complete sequence.

The Viterbi algorithm can efficiently find that sequence for a linear-chain CRF. How do neural networks and CRFs work together? A contextual encoder such as BERT can produce token representations.

A classification head produces emission scores for possible labels.

A CRF then accounts for label transitions.

So we get:

Tokens → Contextual encoder → Tag scores → CRF → Valid structured prediction

This combines learned semantic representations with explicit output-structure modeling. Is a CRF always useful? No.

Modern contextual encoders are already powerful, and independent token classification can work extremely well.

A CRF adds complexity and may offer limited improvement depending on the task.

It's most attractive when output-label dependencies are meaningful and the training data provides enough information to learn them. Evaluation must happen at the right level For NER, token-level accuracy can be misleading.

Suppose a model correctly labels most non-entity tokens but gets entity boundaries wrong.

Its token accuracy may look good while actual entity extraction is poor.

Span-level precision, recall and F1 are usually more informative.

The evaluation unit must match what the user actually needs.

Question answering — From recognizing information to producing answers

Question Answering (QA) introduces another important NLP objective.

The model receives a question and must produce or identify an answer.

There are several different formulations. Extractive QA The answer must be a span of a provided passage.

Example:

Passage: "Alan Turing was born in London in 1912."

Question: "Where was Alan Turing born?"

Answer: "London"

An extractive model commonly predicts start and end positions for the answer span.

The task is constrained by the provided text. Generative QA The model generates an answer in its own words.

It may paraphrase, combine information or use knowledge from pretraining.

This is more flexible but introduces greater risks of unsupported content. Open-domain QA The answer may not be present in a single provided passage.

The system may need to retrieve relevant documents before producing an answer.

This connects QA to information retrieval. Answerability matters Suppose the passage says: "The study evaluated 12 datasets."

And we ask: "Which university funded the study?"

The passage doesn't establish that information.

A system should be able to recognize when the available evidence is insufficient.

Otherwise, it may generate a plausible but unsupported answer.

This becomes a major concern in RAG systems and modern assistant evaluation.

Good QA isn't just finding or generating an answer. It's identifying what the available evidence can actually support.

Information retrieval — Finding the right evidence

Language understanding becomes especially useful when combined with search.

Suppose we have one million scientific papers.

The user asks: "Find studies showing that argument identification models fail to generalize across datasets."

We need to identify relevant documents efficiently.

This is an information-retrieval problem.

We studied three major retrieval approaches. Sparse retrieval: BM25 BM25 is a traditional lexical retrieval method.

It ranks documents using weighted term matches, with adjustments for term frequency and document length.

A common form is: BM25⁡(q,d)=∑t∈qIDF⁡(t)f(t,d)(k1+1)f(t,d)+k1(1−b+b∣d∣/∣d∣‾)\boxed{ \operatorname{BM25}(q,d) = \sum_{t\in q} \operatorname{IDF}(t) \frac{f(t,d)(k_1+1)} {f(t,d)+k_1(1-b+b|d|/\overline{|d|})} }

The important ideas are more useful than memorizing the equation.

Rare terms are informative.

Matching a highly specific phrase can provide stronger evidence than matching a very common word.

Term frequency saturates.

Repeating a query word 100 times shouldn't make a document 100 times more relevant than one containing it once.

Document length matters.

Long documents naturally contain more terms, so BM25 adjusts for length. When does BM25 work well? BM25 is often strong for exact terminology.

Suppose the query mentions:

RoBERTa, Touché 2026, or macro-F1.

A lexical retriever can find documents containing those exact strings.

Dense semantic retrieval may sometimes struggle with rare identifiers, abbreviations, numbers or names. Dense retrieval A dense retriever uses a learned encoder to map queries and documents into vectors. q=fθ(query)q=f_\theta(\text{query})

d=gϕ(document)d=g_\phi(\text{document})

We then compare vectors using dot product or cosine similarity.

This allows retrieval even when the query and document use different words.

For example:

Query: "Models that struggle when tested on unfamiliar datasets."

Document: "Cross-corpus transfer reveals substantial degradation under distribution shift."

A dense retriever may recognize the semantic relationship despite limited word overlap. The limitation of dense retrieval Semantic similarity isn't always sufficient for relevance.

A query about: "Studies where treatment did not improve survival"

may be confused with documents discussing treatments that did improve survival.

The topics are similar, but the crucial conclusion differs.

Dense retrieval can also struggle with exact codes, rare names and fine-grained numerical distinctions. Hybrid retrieval This motivates combining sparse and dense retrieval.

BM25 supplies strong lexical matching.

Dense retrieval supplies semantic matching.

Together, they can complement each other.

But their raw scores often aren't directly comparable.

A BM25 score of 15 and a cosine similarity of 0.8 live on different scales. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) RRF combines ranked result lists rather than directly combining their raw scores.

A standard form is: RRF⁡(d)=∑r∈R1k+rank⁡r(d)\boxed{ \operatorname{RRF}(d)= \sum_{r\in R} \frac1{k+\operatorname{rank}_r(d)} }

Where RR is the collection of retrieval systems.

A document ranked highly by both BM25 and dense retrieval receives a stronger combined score.

The advantage is that we don't need to calibrate incompatible score magnitudes.

RRF combines rankings, not semantic representations.

Reranking — Retrieve broadly, judge carefully

Why not use a powerful Transformer to compare every query with every document?

Because it would be expensive.

Suppose we have one million documents.

A cross-encoder that jointly processes the query and each document would require one million pairwise model evaluations per query.

That isn't practical for most systems.

Instead, we use a multi-stage pipeline.

Stage 1: A fast retriever finds a shortlist, perhaps the top 100 documents.

Stage 2: A more expensive reranker examines those candidates carefully. Bi-encoder versus cross-encoder A bi-encoder encodes queries and documents separately.

Document embeddings can be precomputed and indexed.

This makes large-scale retrieval efficient.

A cross-encoder jointly processes the query and document, allowing richer token-level interactions.

It can make finer relevance judgments, but it generally requires separate computation for each query-document pair. Example Query: "Studies showing no improvement from data simplification."

Candidate A: "Simplification improved accuracy on all datasets."

Candidate B: "Simplification did not consistently improve accuracy across datasets."

Both discuss the same topic.

A dense retriever may consider both relevant.

A cross-encoder can potentially better distinguish which candidate matches the query's specific condition. The recall–precision trade-off First-stage retrieval should aim to include relevant documents among its candidates.

Reranking then improves the ordering.

But there's a hard limitation:

A reranker cannot recover a relevant document that the retriever never selected.

If the correct document isn't in the top 100 candidates, no reranking of those 100 can find it.

This is why retrieval evaluation should include recall at the candidate-generation stage.

RAG — Combining retrieval with language generation

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines an information-retrieval system with a generative language model.

The typical workflow is:

Question → Retrieve documents → Select relevant passages → Give them to an LLM → Generate an answer

Why is this powerful?

Because the language model doesn't need to rely exclusively on information stored in its parameters.

It can access relevant external evidence at inference time. Parametric versus non-parametric knowledge Parametric knowledge is information represented through learned model parameters.

Non-parametric knowledge is information supplied from external sources, such as retrieved documents.

RAG allows the system to use both.

For example, a model may understand how scientific papers are structured from pretraining.

But it can retrieve a newly published paper to answer questions about its specific experiments. RAG does not automatically make the answer correct Suppose the retriever finds the right scientific paper.

The language model might still misunderstand a table, misinterpret a negation or invent a citation.

Conversely, a model might produce the correct answer despite receiving irrelevant documents, relying instead on its pretrained knowledge.

Therefore, RAG has at least two major sources of failure.

Retrieval failure: Relevant evidence wasn't selected.

Generation failure: The model received appropriate evidence but failed to use it correctly.

There can also be evidence-quality failures, where a retrieved document is inaccurate or unreliable. Faithfulness versus factual correctness This is one of the most important distinctions in modern NLP evaluation.

Factual correctness: Is the claim actually true?

Faithfulness: Is the claim supported by the supplied evidence?

An answer can be faithful to a false document while remaining factually incorrect.

Or it can be factually correct but unsupported by the retrieved passages.

So a rigorous RAG evaluation should examine: - Retrieval relevance and coverage. - Answer correctness. - Evidence faithfulness. - Citation support. - Appropriate abstention when evidence is insufficient. Chunking is also an information-design problem Long documents are often divided into passages before indexing.

Small chunks are precise but may separate information that should be interpreted together.

Large chunks preserve more context but increase retrieval and generation costs and can introduce irrelevant material.

For scientific papers, splitting a result statement from its qualifying conditions can be especially harmful.

The best chunking strategy depends on what information must remain together to answer the intended questions. A connection to our security volume Retrieved documents are external data, not automatically authorized instructions.

A RAG system must use retrieved text as evidence without allowing instructions inside that text to override the user's request or application permissions.

That's the prompt-injection boundary we studied in Modern LLMs.

Annotation and evaluation — What exactly counts as the correct label?

Now we reach one of the most important ideas in the entire NLP course.

Suppose we're building an argument-identification model.

We want to classify text as argumentative or non-argumentative.

Consider: "The government should invest more in public transportation."

That looks like an argumentative claim.

But now consider: "The results indicate a substantial improvement."

Is it argumentative?

The answer depends on the dataset's definition of argumentation.

One dataset may consider scientific claims argumentative.

Another may require an explicit stance in a controversy.

A third may annotate only claims supported by premises.

The label isn't defined by the words alone. It is also defined by the annotation guidelines. Annotation guidelines are part of the task A dataset represents the interaction of several factors: Observed label=f(text,context,annotation policy)\boxed{ \text{Observed label} = f(\text{text},\text{context},\text{annotation policy}) }

This is a conceptual relation, not a claim that all annotators are deterministic.

The same text can receive different labels under different annotation policies.

That doesn't necessarily mean one dataset is wrong.

They may be measuring different operational definitions. Label quality Annotation projects should consider: - Whether the guidelines are clear. - Whether annotators agree. - Whether difficult cases are documented. - Whether contextual information is available. - Whether label boundaries are consistent. Inter-annotator agreement can help diagnose ambiguity.

But agreement isn't equivalent to validity.

Two annotators can agree consistently while following a flawed or overly narrow guideline. Why context matters Consider: "Absolutely."

Without context, it is difficult to determine whether this is an argument, agreement or ordinary conversational response.

But if the previous message makes a political claim, "Absolutely" may express agreement with a stance.

A sentence-only classifier may not have enough information to make the intended distinction.

This creates a task-design decision.

Do we classify sentences independently?

Do we provide surrounding conversation?

Do we include dataset-specific labeling guidance?

These aren't merely formatting choices. They change the information available to the model.

Domain shift and cross-dataset generalization

Finally, we connected NLP modeling with one of the most important research problems: generalization beyond the training distribution.

Suppose we train an argument classifier on scientific abstracts.

It performs well on scientific abstracts.

Now we evaluate it on Reddit discussions.

Performance drops dramatically.

Why?

Because the model may have learned patterns associated with scientific writing: - Formal sentence structure. - Explicit research claims. - Technical vocabulary. - Conventional evidence statements. Reddit discussions have different vocabulary, conversational structure and argument conventions.

The model's training distribution doesn't fully match the target distribution. Different forms of shift Input or covariate shift: The distribution of input text changes.

Label-distribution shift: The proportions of labels change.

Conditional or concept shift: The relationship between inputs and labels changes.

In NLP, guideline differences can create an additional complication.

Two datasets may operationalize the labels differently, so the desired classification function itself changes.

For example, one dataset might treat a scientific finding as an argument while another labels only explicit persuasion as argumentative. Why pooled accuracy can hide failures Suppose our model has: Dataset Accuracy Scientific abstracts 92% Online debates 62% Product reviews 78%

If the scientific dataset contains 90% of all test examples, pooled accuracy may look strong.

But that doesn't mean the model generalizes well across all three domains.

We should inspect individual dataset results and choose aggregation methods appropriate to the research question. Macro versus micro aggregation Macro averaging gives datasets, classes or groups equal weight at the relevant aggregation level.

Micro aggregation combines underlying counts before computing the metric.

The distinction is essential.

If the goal is to evaluate performance across different corpora, equal-weight dataset aggregation may reveal failures hidden by pooled scores dominated by large corpora.

But a pooled metric may be appropriate for a deployment population where the observed dataset proportions reflect real traffic.

There is no universally correct aggregation strategy. It depends on what population or generalization claim we're trying to evaluate. Why random train/test splitting can be misleading Suppose sentences from the same document appear in both training and test sets.

The model may exploit document-specific vocabulary or repeated content.

Its test score could overestimate performance on genuinely unseen documents.

For a stronger evaluation, we may need document-level, conversation-level, source-level or temporal splits.

Similarly, if we use target-dataset validation examples to select hyperparameters or choose models, that isn't the same setting as completely unseen zero-shot cross-dataset transfer.

Both experiments can be legitimate, but they answer different questions. Does a larger Transformer solve domain shift? Not automatically.

A larger model may have stronger representations and broader pretraining coverage.

But it can still learn shortcuts from the source dataset or fail to understand a target dataset's annotation policy.

Possible approaches include domain adaptation, broader training mixtures, guideline-conditioned inference, calibration, model ensembling and task-specific evaluation.

The key is to identify which kind of shift is causing the failure.

A model shouldn't be made more complicated before we've checked whether the datasets are actually defining the same task.

Part I conclusion — The complete NLP pipeline

The whole volume can be understood as a progression:

Raw language → Tokenization → Numerical representations → Contextual modeling → Task-specific predictions → Retrieval and generation → Evaluation under distribution shift

Each stage solves a problem created by the previous one.

Tokenization makes text computationally manageable.

Sparse representations capture lexical evidence.

Embeddings represent statistical relationships between words.

Contextual models account for how meaning changes with surrounding text.

Structured prediction models learn relationships between output labels.

Retrieval systems locate evidence outside the model.

RAG combines external evidence with generation.

And rigorous evaluation determines whether the entire system actually performs the task correctly on new data.

The central NLP lesson is that representation, context, task definition and evaluation cannot be separated.

Part II — Six real-world interview questions

These questions test your ability to diagnose NLP systems, choose appropriate methods and reason about generalization.

Question 1 — Your new tokenizer makes the model slower

Scenario: You're adapting a language model for scientific documents.

You replace its tokenizer with a new vocabulary that segments scientific terms more efficiently.

The average paper now uses 25% fewer tokens.

You expect training and inference to become cheaper, but performance deteriorates substantially.

Why?

Answer:

Reducing token count isn't automatically an improvement.

The first thing I'd investigate is whether the new tokenizer is compatible with the pretrained model's token embeddings and output head.

A pretrained language model has learned representations associated with its original token IDs.

If we replace the tokenizer, those IDs can change meaning.

The original embedding matrix may no longer represent the new tokens correctly.

Even if we resize the embeddings, newly introduced tokens require learning useful representations.

That can be expensive and data-intensive.

I would distinguish two objectives:

Efficiency: Can we reduce the number of tokens without sacrificing quality?

Compatibility: Can the existing pretrained model meaningfully interpret the resulting token IDs?

If we're training a language model from scratch, tokenizer design is a natural part of model development.

If we're adapting an existing checkpoint, retaining the original tokenizer is often the safer starting point.

Interview principle: Tokenization is part of the learned model interface, not an independent text-compression step that can always be replaced after pretraining.

Question 2 — BM25 beats your state-of-the-art dense retriever

Scenario: You're building a search engine for scientific papers.

A modern dense embedding model performs well on general semantic-search benchmarks.

But on your research-paper collection, BM25 retrieves the correct papers more reliably.

The queries often contain exact model names, dataset identifiers and experimental terminology.

Is your dense retriever necessarily defective?

Answer:

No.

The dataset may favor lexical matching.

Rare identifiers such as dataset names, model versions and technical abbreviations can be highly informative.

BM25 rewards exact matches of distinctive terms.

A dense model, meanwhile, compresses meaning into vectors and may emphasize broad semantic similarity.

That can cause confusion between documents discussing related topics but different technical entities.

I'd analyze errors by query type.

For example, separate exact-identifier queries from conceptual paraphrase queries.

Then I'd evaluate a hybrid system combining BM25 and dense retrieval.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion would be a reasonable starting point for combining rankings.

After retrieving a sufficiently broad candidate set, a cross-encoder reranker could improve ordering.

But I'd first verify that the correct document appears in the candidates at all.

Interview principle: Semantic retrieval isn't always superior to lexical retrieval. Exact matching and conceptual similarity are complementary capabilities.

Question 3 — Lower perplexity, worse downstream performance

Scenario: You compare two language models.

Model A achieves lower perplexity on a held-out text corpus.

Model B performs better on scientific claim classification and question answering.

How can this happen?

Answer:

Perplexity measures how much probability the model assigns to the evaluation text.

It doesn't directly measure task accuracy, factual grounding or instruction-following ability.

Model A might be better at predicting the surface distribution of the held-out corpus.

Model B might have representations or post-training that are better suited to the target tasks.

Differences in pretraining data, architecture, fine-tuning and evaluation formats can all affect downstream performance.

I'd also verify that the perplexity numbers are comparable.

For example, using different tokenizers can make raw token-level perplexity comparisons misleading.

The appropriate evaluation depends on the intended application.

If we're choosing a model for scientific claim classification, held-out classification metrics are more directly relevant than language-model perplexity alone.

Interview principle: Improving a proxy objective doesn't guarantee improvement on every downstream task.

Question 4 — Your NER model has high token accuracy but poor entity extraction

Scenario: You're extracting organization names from academic papers.

The model reports 97% token accuracy.

But users complain that organization names are often incomplete or incorrectly segmented.

What's happening?

Answer:

Token accuracy can be dominated by the many tokens that don't belong to entities.

A model that labels almost everything as O may achieve a deceptively high accuracy if entities are rare.

The users care about complete entity spans.

For example, suppose the correct entity is:

"Bauhaus-Universität Weimar"

But the model extracts only:

"Bauhaus-Universität"

Even though most individual token labels may be correct, the extracted entity is incomplete.

I'd inspect span-level precision, recall and F1.

I'd also analyze boundary errors, tokenization alignment, entity-length effects and the consistency of BIO tags.

A CRF might help if invalid label transitions are a recurring problem, but it wouldn't automatically fix missing contextual information or inconsistent annotations.

Interview principle: Evaluate structured predictions at the level of the actual output object, not merely at the level of individual token decisions.

Question 5 — Your RAG assistant confidently invents findings

Scenario: You build a scientific question-answering system.

The retriever returns relevant papers, but the assistant sometimes claims that a study demonstrated a statistically significant improvement when the paper actually reported mixed results.

Would you start by replacing the retrieval model?

Answer:

Not immediately.

I'd separate retrieval errors from generation errors.

First, inspect whether the retrieved passages actually contain the relevant findings and qualifications.

If the evidence is missing, retrieval or chunking may be responsible.

If the evidence is present but the language model misinterprets it, the problem is more likely in answer generation, evidence selection or evaluation.

For example, the system may have retrieved a passage saying:

"The method improved performance on Dataset A but showed no consistent benefit elsewhere."

If the model answers:

"The method consistently improved performance across datasets,"

then the evidence was available, but the model failed to use it faithfully.

I'd evaluate claim-level support, negation handling and whether source citations genuinely support the generated statements.

I'd also consider prompting or structured extraction that requires the model to identify results and qualifications before producing a summary.

A model that says "the paper doesn't establish that conclusion" when evidence is insufficient can be more reliable than one that always produces a definitive answer.

Interview principle: Retrieval relevance, evidence quality and generation faithfulness are separate failure points. Diagnose the stage before changing the system.

Question 6 — Your argument classifier collapses on a new dataset

Scenario: You've trained an argument-identification model on scientific abstracts.

It reaches macro-F1 of 0.86 on its source test set.

On an online-discussion dataset, macro-F1 falls to 0.58.

A colleague suggests using a much larger LLM and immediately fine-tuning it on the target test distribution.

What would you do instead?

Answer:

I'd first investigate the source of the generalization gap.

There are at least three possibilities.

Input shift: Scientific abstracts and online discussions use different vocabulary, sentence structure and discourse conventions.

Label-policy shift: The datasets may define argumentative content differently.

Context shift: The target task may require conversational context that isn't available in the source dataset or current model input.

I'd examine annotation guidelines and sample examples from both datasets.

For instance, one corpus might label scientific findings as arguments, while another requires an explicit persuasive stance.

If the guidelines differ, the model isn't necessarily failing to recognize the same underlying concept. It may be applying the source dataset's policy to a target with different labeling rules.

Next, I'd inspect class distributions, confusion matrices and performance by text type.

I'd compare simple baselines, contextual encoders and potentially guideline-conditioned models before assuming a larger architecture is required.

Most importantly, I'd preserve a clean evaluation protocol.

If I use labeled target development data to select the model or tune hyperparameters, I'd report that as target-adapted evaluation—not unseen zero-shot transfer.

I would never train on target test labels and still describe the resulting score as an independent test result.

Finally, I'd report performance by dataset alongside any pooled or macro-aggregated results.

A strong pooled score can hide failure on smaller or more difficult domains.

Interview principle: Cross-dataset NLP performance depends on the data distribution, available context, labeling policy and evaluation design—not just the model's parameter count.

The six principles to remember from Natural Language Processing 1. Text representation is a design decision. Tokenization, sparse vectors and embeddings preserve different kinds of information.

  1. Lexical similarity and semantic similarity are complementary. BM25, dense retrieval and reranking solve different parts of the search problem.

  2. Meaning depends on context and structure. Static word embeddings cannot fully represent context-dependent meanings, while sequence models and contextual encoders can model richer relationships.

  3. The training objective defines what the model learns. Language modeling, classification, structured prediction, retrieval and generation require different objectives and evaluation procedures.

  4. RAG separates information storage from generation, but doesn't guarantee correctness. Retrieval quality, evidence support and answer faithfulness must be evaluated independently.

  5. Labels and distributions define generalization. A model cannot be judged independently of dataset composition, annotation guidelines, target-domain context and evaluation protocol.

How Natural Language Processing connects to Modern LLMs Our first three volumes establish the ingredients of modern LLM systems:

Deep Learning Basics: How parameters are optimized.

Deep Learning Architectures: How architectural structure determines information flow.

Natural Language Processing: How language becomes tokens, representations, tasks and retrievable evidence.

Modern LLMs combines those ideas at scale.

A modern LLM uses the tokenization and language-modeling principles from Natural Language Processing, the Transformer architecture from Deep Learning Architectures, and the optimization principles from Deep Learning Basics.

It then adds large-scale pretraining, efficient inference, instruction tuning, preference optimization, agentic tool use, security and system-level evaluation.

The biggest conceptual transition is this:

Traditional NLP often builds a model for a defined language task. Modern LLM engineering increasingly starts with a broadly pretrained model and adapts, guides or extends it into a complete task-solving system.
